name: China's recurrent reunification
what: After every collapse a single dynasty rebuilt one empire over the Chinese core: Sui 589, Song 960-979, Yuan 1279, Ming 1368, Qing 1644-1683.
why: Scheidel calls this the great East-West contrast: Rome never came back, the Chinese empire always did.

name: Europe's lasting political fragmentation
what: After Rome no power ever again ruled more than a fraction of Latin Europe for long; Charlemagne, the Habsburgs and Napoleon all failed.
why: Scheidel argues this 'competitive fragmentation' was the precondition for modern growth.

name: Europe's tournament of warring states
what: Rival European states fought almost constantly, pouring revenue into gunpowder armies and navies.
why: Hoffman's tournament model: frequent war among similar rivals drove fast military learning.

name: Europe's cross-border market for ideas
what: The Republic of Letters: scholars who could flee one prince to another and publish across borders.
why: Mokyr's mechanism linking fragmentation to the Enlightenment and industrial technology.

name: The European scientific revolution
what: From Copernicus (1543) to Newton's Principia (1687): mathematised, experimental natural philosophy.
why: The benchmark against which the Needham question asks why China, ahead for centuries, did not do the same.

name: Britain's shallow coal and the escape from wood
what: English coal output rose from around 200,000 tons a year in the 1560s to roughly 15 million tons by 1800, close to the cities and the sea.
why: Wrigley and Pomeranz see coal as the way out of the organic economy's land limit.

name: The North Sea's high-wage economy
what: After the Black Death, wages in London and Amsterdam stayed far above subsistence; by the 1700s they were the highest in the world.
why: Allen argues dear labour and cheap coal made labour-saving machines pay in Britain first.

name: The British Industrial Revolution
what: Cotton mills, steam engines and coked iron turned Britain into the first economy with sustained per-capita growth.

name: The Great Divergence
what: The opening of the income gap between north-western Europe and East Asia; when it opened is the argument.
why: Rishi's question: when did Western Europe actually become richer than China?

name: The Tianbao frontier wars
what: Emperor Xuanzong's armies fought Tibet, the Khitan, Nanzhao in Yunnan (751, 754) and the Abbasids at Talas (751).
why: The wars built the huge standing frontier armies that An Lushan would turn on the court.

name: Tang frontier commands (jiedushi)
what: By 742 some 490,000 professional troops stood in ten frontier commands, most of them on the northern border; An Lushan held three at once.
why: Pulleyblank's starting point: the dynasty armed its frontier generals and disarmed the centre.

name: Feud between An Lushan and Yang Guozhong
what: Yang Guifei's cousin Yang Guozhong became chief minister in 752 and accused An Lushan of plotting rebellion.

name: The long drought of the Uyghur empire
what: Tree rings show a severe drought lasting nearly seven decades during the Uyghur empire (744-840).

name: An Lushan rebellion
what: The Sogdian-Turkic general An Lushan rose at Fanyang in 755, took Luoyang and Chang'an, and the war dragged on until 763.
why: The hinge of Chinese history: the cosmopolitan aristocratic Tang gave way to a fiscal, commercial, regional China.

name: Collapse of the Tang household registers
what: Registered population fell from about 52.9 million (755) to about 17 million (760).
why: Durand argues most of the 'missing' 36 million escaped the registers rather than died.

name: Tang salt monopoly
what: From 758 the court sold salt at a monopoly price; by the 770s the salt commission supplied around half of central cash revenue.
why: The dynasty survived by taxing trade instead of registered peasants.

name: The two-tax reform of 780
what: Yang Yan replaced the per-head equal-field taxes with two seasonal levies on property and land.
why: The end of the state's attempt to allot land: China's tax state now followed wealth, not heads.

name: The autonomous northeastern provinces
what: Former rebel generals in Hebei kept their armies, passed their posts to sons and paid little to the court.

name: Weak summer monsoons of the late Tang
what: Lake and cave records from south China show a run of weak summer monsoons in the 9th and early 10th centuries.

name: Huang Chao rebellion
what: A salt smuggler's army crossed China, sacked Guangzhou (879) and Chang'an (881).
why: Tackett shows its armies wiped out the capital-based great clans.

name: Destruction of the medieval aristocracy
what: The great Tang clans, concentrated in Chang'an and Luoyang, were massacred in the 880s and 900s.
why: It cleared the way for the Song examination elite.

name: China's population moves south
what: The share of registered households south of the Huai-Han line rose from under half in the mid-Tang to around two thirds by 1080.
why: Rice paddies of the Yangzi made the Song economic revolution possible.

name: Champa rice spread in the lower Yangzi
what: In 1012 the Song court distributed drought-resistant, early-ripening Champa rice seed to the Yangzi and Huai provinces.

name: The Song economic revolution
what: Rice, canals, markets, printing, paper money and coal-fired iron made Song China the richest and most urban society on earth.
why: Elvin's 'medieval economic revolution' and the high point in Broadberry, Guan and Li's GDP series.

name: The Northern Song iron and coal boom
what: Hartwell estimated iron output at about 125,000 tons in 1078, much of it smelted with coal in Hebei and Shandong to supply Kaifeng.
why: A level England reached only in the 18th century, and the case for a Song 'industrial revolution'.

name: The first state paper money (jiaozi)
what: In 1024 the Song state took over the merchants' iron-cash notes of Sichuan and issued jiaozi, the world's first government paper money.

name: Wang Anshi's New Policies
what: State loans to farmers, trade bureaus, militia and a tea-and-horse monopoly that drained Sichuan.
why: A state-led bid to mobilise the commercial economy for war against the Xi Xia and Liao.

name: China's stagnant, then falling, income per head
what: In Broadberry, Guan and Li's series China's GDP per head hovers between about 1,200 and 1,550 (2011 dollars) from the Northern Song to 1700, then falls to about 860 by 1850.
why: The early-divergence answer to Rishi's question.

name: The high-level equilibrium trap
what: Elvin's model: a farming system so efficient and populous that cheap labour left nothing to gain from labour-saving machines.

name: China's missing scientific and industrial breakthrough
what: Song China led in printing, gunpowder, the compass, iron and astronomy, yet modern science and the factory took off in Europe.
why: This is the Needham question.

name: Late 12th-century drought in Mongolia
what: Tree rings from Siberian pine show severe drought on the Mongolian plateau in the 1180s.
why: The hard years in which Temujin rose amid tribal war.

name: The Mongol pluvial
what: Fifteen consecutive years of above-average rainfall and mild temperatures, unmatched in the 1,112-year tree-ring record.
why: More grass, more horses and livestock: Pederson and colleagues' fuel for the conquests.

name: Temujin proclaimed Chinggis Khan
what: The kuriltai on the Onon recognised Temujin as Chinggis Khan over the united steppe tribes.

name: The Mongol conquests
what: From the Xi Xia (1209) and the Jin (1211) to Khwarazm, Rus, Hungary, Baghdad and finally the Southern Song (1279).

name: Population collapse of north China under the Mongol conquest
what: Registered households in the north fell by most of their number between the Jin census and the Yuan count of the 1230s, and China's population sank from over 100 million to perhaps 60-75 million by 1290.

name: Death of Ogedei Khan
what: The Great Khan died in December 1241 near Karakorum.

name: Wet, cold spring in Hungary, 1242
what: Tree rings and documents show a cold winter then a wet spring that turned the Hungarian plain into marsh.

name: Mongol withdrawal from Hungary
what: Batu's armies left Hungary in spring 1242 after a year of devastation.

name: The Mongol exchange
what: Caravans, envoys, doctors and astronomers moved across a Eurasia under Chinggisid rule.

name: Collapse of Yuan paper money
what: Massive printing of chao to fund the Yellow River works and suppress revolt destroyed the currency by the 1350s.

name: Yellow River breaches of the 1340s
what: The Yellow River broke its dykes in 1344 and wandered for years; 150,000 labourers were drafted in 1351 to fix it.

name: Red Turban rebellion
what: Millenarian White Lotus rebels rose among the dyke conscripts and splintered into warlord regimes; one, Zhu Yuanzhang, founded the Ming.

name: Ming maritime ban (haijin)
what: The Hongwu emperor forbade private overseas trade; only tribute missions could trade.

name: Ming taxes and markets turn to silver
what: As paper money died, uncoined silver became the money of account; grain taxes were commuted to silver from 1436.

name: Japan's silver boom
what: New cupellation techniques at Iwami and other mines made Japan perhaps a third of world silver output by the early 1600s, most of it bound for China.

name: Ban on private overseas trade lifted at Yuegang
what: The Longqing court licensed Fujian junks to trade in Southeast Asia from Yuegang; Manila became their silver market.

name: The Single Whip reform
what: Zhang Juzheng's empire-wide consolidation of land tax and labour service into one payment in silver.

name: The Liaodong war and its surtaxes
what: After Nurhaci's attack in 1618, surtaxes for the Manchu front were added year after year.

name: Tokugawa expulsion of the Portuguese (sakoku)
what: The 1639 edict expelled the Portuguese, the main carriers of Japanese silver to China.

name: The silver import slump of 1639-1644
what: Atwell's crisis: the Portuguese expulsion from Japan, the 1639 massacre of Chinese in Manila and losses at sea cut silver arrivals just as harvests failed.

name: China's coldest decades: the 1630s-1640s
what: Documentary reconstructions put the 1640s among the coldest decades in China of the last 2,000 years.

name: Late Ming epidemics
what: Epidemics swept the north China plain and reached Beijing in 1643-44, killing a large share of the capital's people and garrison.

name: Late Ming rebellions
what: Mutinous soldiers, laid-off postal workers and starving farmers in Shaanxi grew into the armies of Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong.

name: The Manchu conquest of China
what: From the occupation of Beijing in 1644 to the surrender of Taiwan in 1683.

name: Qing population boom
what: China grew from perhaps 150 million around 1700 to about 430 million by 1850.

name: Kangxi's freeze of the tax quota
what: The 1712 edict fixed the head-tax quota forever; the land tax stayed nearly flat in silver while population tripled.

name: Qing ever-normal granaries
what: A network of state granaries that at its 18th-century peak held tens of millions of shi of grain to damp prices and feed famine areas.

name: The Yangzi delta's land and fuel squeeze
what: Dense, commercial Jiangnan ran short of wood, fertiliser and land; growth came from more work per acre, not new energy.

name: White Lotus rebellion
what: A millenarian rising in the Han river highlands that cost the Qing nine years and some 200 million taels.

name: China's silver drain
what: From the 1820s silver left China; the price of silver in copper cash roughly doubled between 1800 and the late 1840s, raising the real weight of taxes paid in silver.

name: The First Opium War
what: Britain's war to force open the opium trade, ended by the Treaty of Nanjing (1842).

name: Hong Xiuquan's visions
what: A Hakka schoolteacher who failed the exams four times read a Christian tract and decided he was Christ's younger brother.

name: Taiping civil war
what: The Heavenly Kingdom ruled the lower Yangzi from Nanjing for eleven years; the war killed at least 20 million people.

name: Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army
what: A regional army of Hunan gentry and peasants, paid by local trade taxes (lijin), that broke the Taiping.

name: Anglo-French intervention against the Taiping
what: After 1860 British and French forces, and Ward's and Gordon's mercenaries, defended Shanghai and helped retake the delta.

name: Depopulation of the lower Yangzi
what: Whole counties of Jiangnan, China's richest region, lost most of their people to massacre, famine and disease.

name: The Tongzhi Restoration and Self-Strengthening
what: Arsenals, shipyards and a revived Confucian order under regional governors-general.

name: Provincial power after the Taiping
what: Governors-general with their own armies and revenues held the real power in late Qing China.

name: Tokugawa rural commerce and by-employment
what: Farm families spun, wove, brewed and reeled silk for markets; literacy and small-scale skills spread through the villages.

name: Perry's Black Ships
what: An American squadron forced the shogunate to sign the Treaty of Kanagawa (1854).

name: Japan opens its treaty ports
what: Under the 1858 treaties Yokohama, Nagasaki and Hakodate opened to foreign trade in 1859, with tariffs capped near 5 percent from 1866.

name: Japan's raw silk export boom
what: Raw silk, Japan's first great export, overtook China's in world markets by about 1905.

name: Collapse of the shogunate's authority
what: Treaties signed without imperial consent, inflation and rebel domains (Choshu, Satsuma) undid the Tokugawa.

name: The Meiji Restoration
what: In January 1868 Satsuma and Choshu troops proclaimed the restoration of imperial rule; the shogunate's forces lost the Boshin war by 1869.

name: Meiji land tax reform
what: A fixed money tax of 3 percent of assessed land value replaced domain rice levies.

name: The 1872 education ordinance (Gakusei)
what: Universal elementary schooling on a French model; enrolment passed 90 percent by the early 1900s.

name: Meiji railway building
what: From the Tokyo-Yokohama line (1872) to a national trunk network.

name: Meiji industrialisation
what: Cotton spinning, silk reeling, shipbuilding and mining made Japan Asia's first industrial economy.

name: First Sino-Japanese War
what: Japan's modern army and navy beat the Qing in Korea and at the Yalu and Weihaiwei; China ceded Taiwan.

name: Bai Juyi
what: Tang poet and official, famous for plain-language satirical ballads.

name: Arthur Waley
what: British translator of Chinese and Japanese literature.

name: Juan González de Mendoza
what: Spanish Augustinian friar, author of the first European bestseller on Ming China (1585).

name: Augustus F. Lindley
what: British adventurer who served the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.

name: Ernest Satow
what: British interpreter and diplomat in Japan during the Meiji Restoration.
